desc.samogon.wash: Sweet unfermented wort: not a drink yet, but the base for fermentation.
desc.samogon.braga: Braga is as old as farming: Babylonians fermented it, and Russian villages made it from anything that would ferment. Peasants called it 'bread wine', though it contained less bread than optimism. Drinkable, yes, but distilling it is the next step towards civilisation.
desc.samogon.moonshine: Russian double distillation was known by the 15th century: the treasury fumed, the village hid the still in the banya, and the drink survived. 'Samogon' means 'I distil it myself' — perhaps the most honest marketing in history. Cut the heads and avoid the tax office.
desc.samogon.chacha: Georgians have run chacha from grape pomace for centuries: the ripe grapes go to wine, and whatever is left goes to chacha. No cluster is wasted, and that is not greed but respect for the harvest. Chacha is strong, direct and as warm as a Caucasian toast.
desc.samogon.whiskey: Irish monks called whiskey 'water of life' (uisce beatha) in the 12th century, and the name stuck. Later the Scots added peat, the Americans corn and charred barrels, and tax inspectors added their opinion. The drink now has its own holiday and its own morning-after headache.
desc.samogon.rum: Rum was invented in the 17th-century Caribbean so molasses, a sugar-making waste, would not be thrown away. Pirates valued its strength, the Royal Navy the fact that it could dilute both water and morale. Today rum lives in cocktails and neat glasses, but its history remains piratical.
desc.samogon.brandy: Brandy is the Dutch sailors' 'burnt wine' (brandewijn): they distilled wine so it would survive the voyage. It was first sold as medicine, which explains a great deal — the taste was such that illness preferred to retreat. The oak cask later turned the medicine into a pleasure.
desc.samogon.cognac: Cognac appeared in 17th-century France when winemakers decided distilling wine was more profitable than waiting for it to survive the sea crossing. Two distillations, an oak cask and strict regional rules did the rest. Today cognac is an excuse to speak slowly and look into the distance.
desc.samogon.calvados: Normandy has distilled calvados from cider since the 16th century: there were so many apples that cider became a logistics problem. Locals worked it out — if the apples will not fit in the cellar, distil them and put them back, more compactly. The result is soft, orchard-scented and mischievous.
desc.samogon.scotch: Scotch first appears in the Exchequer Rolls of 1494: monks distilled it 'for health', and the tax office preserved the recipe. Peat gave the famous smoke, the harsh climate gave a reason to drink slowly. Scots and Irish will argue about whose whisky is right — that, too, is tradition.
desc.samogon.cachaca: Cachaca has been distilled in 16th-century Brazil from sugar cane brought by the Portuguese. The locals quickly found cane interesting in more than one form and added a still. Today cachaca is the base of the caipirinha and a matter of national pride; do not mention rum in its presence.
desc.samogon.potato: Potato spirit became fashionable in 18th-century Prussia: there was more potato than there were ideas for it. People ate it, fed it to livestock, then learned to distil it — and found the most versatile way to store a harvest. The taste is neutral, the history is pure practicality.
desc.samogon.beet: Beet spirit was born in Europe when Napoleon cut off cane sugar. The beet saved the confectioners and, incidentally, the distilleries: sugar was found where nobody expected it. The drink turned out faintly sweet and unusual — exactly as befits an invention born of military necessity.
desc.samogon.mead: Mead is older than writing: Vikings and ancient Slavs drank it, and put in so much honey that the bees took it personally. It was food, medicine, currency and a good reason for a quarrel all at once. Distilling mead came later, but the respect for bees remains unchanged.
desc.samogon.cocoa: The Aztecs drank cocoa — without sugar, but with chilli and foam. Europeans added sugar, the Spanish added secrecy, and confectioners added milk. Cocoa distillate is a new and slightly mischievous idea, but the drink's history is very serious: it was once both bitter medicine and luxury.
desc.samogon.melon: Melon distillates are rare even among fruit spirits: France makes eau-de-vie from fruit, but the melon is usually eaten before it reaches the still. Whoever waits gets a pale, green-fruited drink that smells of summer. Sceptics call it very expensive water with degrees, but sceptics rarely get a second glass.
desc.samogon.carrot: Carrot spirit is a drink for the desperate: wartime Britain made 'beer' from carrots, so distilling was the logical next step. Carrots store well, grow cheaply and bring an earthy sweetness. The result is not an everyday drink, but it comes with a story worth telling at the table.
desc.samogon.cactus: Cactus spirit is Mexico's answer to the desert: thorny plants have been distilled there for centuries, and cactus is not the worst option. Agave is more famous, but cactus can surprise you: the taste is bright, vegetal and a little prickly. Do not try to repeat it on a windowsill.
desc.samogon.vodka: Vodka was known in Eastern Europe by the 14th-15th centuries and called 'water': first a medicine, then a drink, then a state monopoly. The recipe was simple: distil, filter, and do not argue with the treasury. Purity mattered so much that vodka was judged by the absence of a bouquet.
desc.samogon.spirit: Strong rectified spirit is a child of alchemy: medieval alchemists sought the elixir of life and got ethanol. They advised against drinking it neat, but recommended it as a solvent, medicine and base for experiments. Since then spirit has remained a universal tool — drink and chemical at once.
desc.samogon.gin: Gin began in Holland as 'juniper vodka', and in 18th-century England it took off so hard that the authorities introduced licences and taxes. It did not help: gin became the symbol of London taverns and colonial clubs. What matters is the botanical bundle: juniper, coriander and a readiness to experiment.
desc.samogon.absinthe: Absinthe was nicknamed the 'Green Fairy' in 19th-century Paris: artists, poets and the curious drank it. It was banned for nearly a century and blamed for madness, though strength was the likelier culprit. The fairy returned, and so did the legend — wormwood, anise and a taste of the forbidden.
desc.samogon.liqueur: Liqueurs were invented by monks as medicines: sugar and herbs made the draught tastier and the illness less convincing. The medicine moved from pharmacy to sideboard, and recipes became family secrets. Today a liqueur keeps summer in a bottle: berries, honey, spices and a little sugar for persuasiveness.
desc.samogon.tincture: Tinctures began as medicine: alcohol drew everything useful out of the herbs, and everything else too. In villages this counted as prevention, in pharmacies as science, and at parties as a pleasant addition. The old distillers' rule: do not argue about the benefits before the third glass.

guide.samogon.body: Chain: malt -> wort -> fermentation -> wash -> pot still -> heads/hearts/tails -> reflux column -> filter -> dilution basin -> blend -> aging. The blending table has five slots: berries, honey, beetroot, potato, seeds, herbs, mushrooms and more. Empty-hand right-click opens the machine interface; right-click with an item is the quick manual path. Golden sparkles mean the product is ready. The thermometer and hydrometer report process values. This is a game simulation, not a real production guide.

guide.samogon.page.raw.malt: Malt: grain origin, +4 quality. Base wash about 11.5%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.wheat: Wheat: grain origin, no bonus. Base wash about 11.5%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.sugar: Sugar: sugar origin, -4 quality. Base wash about 13.5%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.berries: Sweet berries: berry origin, +2 quality. Base about 10.5%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.honey: Honey bottle: honey origin, +6 quality, returns the glass bottle. Base about 12.5%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.potato: Potato: potato origin, -2 quality. Base wash about 12%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.beetroot: Beetroot: beetroot origin, no bonus. Base wash about 11%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.cane: Sugar cane: cane origin, +1 quality. Base wash about 13%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.apple: Apple: apple origin, +3 quality. Base wash about 10%%.
guide.samogon.page.raw.summary: One portion -> 2000 units of wort. After fermentation about 1900 units of wash; one jar holds 1000.
guide.samogon.page.raw.tip: Base strength is before temperature. 20 C is best; heat hurts quality and raises impurities.
guide.samogon.page.trouble.title: Troubleshooting
guide.samogon.page.trouble.heat: The tun does not heat: fire or a lit campfire must be directly below it.
guide.samogon.page.trouble.ferment: Fermentation stalled: keep 8-38 C. A campfire warms; ice cools.
guide.samogon.page.trouble.still: The still is silent: wash 100+, heat below, water bucket in the condenser.
guide.samogon.page.trouble.cuts: The still puked: lower the heat, refill coolant, and keep the cuts apart.
guide.samogon.page.trouble.column: The column is weak: feed low wines and heat below; a sieve gives 99.5%%.
guide.samogon.page.trouble.basin: The basin rejects it: spirit must be above 40%%; final volume up to 4000.
guide.samogon.page.trouble.bottle: Cannot bottle: bottle in output. Glow and sparkles mean ready.
guide.samogon.page.trouble.tip: Empty hand: panel. Shift+right-click: quick action. Meters: values.
guide.samogon.page.overview.title: Full cycle
guide.samogon.page.overview.lead: Seven stages, fire and time. From malt to the oak cask.
guide.samogon.page.overview.tip: Empty-hand right-click: panel. Light and sparkles: ready.
guide.samogon.page.mash.title: Wash
guide.samogon.page.mash.step1: Malt into the tun, heat below. 20 sec.
guide.samogon.page.mash.step2: Bottle the wort, then add yeast.
guide.samogon.page.mash.step3: 5 min at 20 °C. Bottle the finished wash.
guide.samogon.page.mash.tip: 8–38 °C is the working range. Heat or cold stalls fermentation.
guide.samogon.page.mash.note: Progress stuck? Check the heat under the tun and the air around the barrel.
guide.samogon.page.still.title: Distilling
guide.samogon.page.still.bar.caption: the cuts come in order
guide.samogon.page.still.step1: Wash into the pot; water in the condenser is required.
guide.samogon.page.still.step3: Change the receiver with the interface button or Shift-right-click.
guide.samogon.page.still.step4: Hearts into a bottle. Heads and tails are technical.
guide.samogon.page.still.note: Light and sparkles mean ready. Do not clear the pot before the cuts are bottled.
guide.samogon.page.clean.title: Cleaning
guide.samogon.page.clean.step1: Any spirit into the column, heat below; choose 1–6 passes.
guide.samogon.page.clean.step2: Strength climbs: 62 → 76 → 85 → 90 → 94 → 96%%. A sieve from the 4th pass reaches 99.5%%.
guide.samogon.page.clean.step3: Spirit and charcoal into the filter.
guide.samogon.page.clean.step4: 30 sec. Check the strength with a hydrometer.
guide.samogon.page.clean.tip: The column takes about 60 sec per pass. Without a sieve it cannot pass 96%%; the sieve works from the 4th pass.
guide.samogon.page.dilute.title: Dilution
guide.samogon.page.dilute.gauge.caption: target 40%% ABV
guide.samogon.page.dilute.step2: A water bucket starts 10 sec of mixing.
guide.samogon.page.dilute.step4: Bottle it for blending or the cask. The basin holds up to 4000 units.
guide.samogon.page.dilute.tip: Hearts or clean spirit only. Never dilute heads and tails.
guide.samogon.page.blend.title: Blending
guide.samogon.page.blend.tag: five additives | up to five effects
guide.samogon.page.blend.ingredients: berries | honey | flowers | herbs | seeds | fruit | spice | seaweed
guide.samogon.page.blend.step2: Fill up to five slots: berries, honey, flowers, herbs, fruit, spice, mushrooms, seaweed and more.
guide.samogon.page.blend.step3: Press "Blend" or Shift+right-click with an empty hand.
guide.samogon.page.blend.tip: Repeating an additive strengthens its effect: five berries give berry V. Mixed additives give up to five level-I effects. Rectified spirit + botanical bundle = gin; add ferns for absinthe; sugar + berries or honey at 40%% = liqueur. Above 60%%: dilute in the basin.

guide.samogon.page.age.step1: Spirit at 4–60%% ABV into the cask.
guide.samogon.page.age.tip: Hearts or blend only, never heads and tails.

desc.samogon.kvass: Kvass is at least a thousand years old: it was brewed in ancient Rus from rusks, bread and whatever was lying about. It outlived invasions, samovars and fizzy drinks, remaining a drink for children and adults. In summer it saved you from heat, in winter it reminded you of summer.
desc.samogon.beer: Beer is older than bread: the Sumerians brewed it in the 3rd millennium BC, and Egyptian builders got it as part of their wages. No wonder the pyramids stand — you can build much on that fuel. Humanity refined the recipe but never changed the point: beer brings people together.
desc.samogon.beer.light: Pale beer is the basic style, brewed since Mesopotamia: cloudy, warm and already honest. Later came pale malt, clean yeast and cold fermentation, and the drink turned clear. The essence stayed the same: malt, water, hops and good company.
desc.samogon.beer.wheat: Wheat beer mattered so much in Bavaria that 16th-century dukes made it a monopoly — and kept the brand. Wheat brings softness and a faint haze, while the yeast brings banana-and-spice aroma. Bavarians still argue about the right wheat beer, but they drink any of them.
desc.samogon.beer.dark: Dark beer came before pale: malt was dried over open fire and darkened on its own. Pale malt was technical progress; dark malt was ancient tradition. The taste is caramel, with a little bitterness and a hint of coffee, especially when the malt is well roasted.
desc.samogon.beer.honey: Honey beer is an ancient hybrid of beer and mead: Egypt knew it, and Scandinavia knew it, where honey was currency. Honey ferments almost completely, leaving roundness and a floral aroma rather than sticky sweetness. The result goes down easily and ends surprisingly quickly.
desc.samogon.beer.berry: Berry beer was brewed in medieval Europe, often instead of hops, which were expensive. Currants, raspberries and cherries saved both the flavour and the budget, adding a tart edge. Modern brewers returned to the idea, no longer to save money but out of love for experiment.
desc.samogon.beer.apple: Apple beer is cider's cousin: England and Normandy added apples to beer when malt was short and the orchard was not. The fruit acidity refreshes, while the malt base keeps the drink from becoming juice. Above all, do not call it cider in front of an English brewer.
desc.samogon.beer.ipa: IPA was made in England for the voyage to India: heavily hopped so it would survive the trip. The hops managed; the sailors not always. Today IPA is less about travel than about a bright hop aroma, firm bitterness and a willingness to argue about hop varieties until morning.
desc.samogon.beer.porter: Porter was named after London porters: they wanted a dark, filling beer, plenty of calories and few questions. In the 18th century it became London's first mass-market beer, brewed in huge batches. Today it is back for anyone who likes chocolate, coffee and a solid foundation.
desc.samogon.beer.pilsner: Pilsner was brewed in Plzen in 1842 and proved so popular that Czechs still call it theirs while the world simply drinks it. Pale malt, soft water and bottom fermentation produced a clear, dry, crisp taste. Since then 'pilsner' has become almost a synonym for pale lager.
desc.samogon.beer.schwarz: Schwarzbier means 'black beer' in German; Thuringia brewed it long before dark malt became fashionable. Unlike porter, it stays dry and clean: the dark colour is there, the heavy sweetness is not. Germans value it for restraint, beer snobs for the chance to show off their pronunciation.
desc.samogon.beer.bock: Bock came from the German town of Einbeck: monks brewed a strong lager to survive Lent. Judging by the name and the strength, they survived cheerfully. Today bock means a full body, malt sweetness and warming power — ideal for winter and for debates about better beer.
tooltip.samogon.beer.mug: Poured into a wooden mug; the mug stays after the last sip.
tooltip.samogon.brewery: Brewery: malt and water → wort, hops → hopped wort; beer ferments in the beer barrel
gui.samogon.brewery.tab.mash.tooltip: Mashing: malt, wheat or roasted malt and a water bucket give beer wort.
gui.samogon.brewery.tab.boil.tooltip: Boiling: wort and hops over heat give hopped wort.
gui.samogon.brewery.tab.kvass.tooltip: Kvass: rusks and a water bucket give kvass wort; it ferments in the beer barrel.
gui.samogon.brewery.hint.heat: Boil: a heat source below the kettle
gui.samogon.brewery.hint.kvass: Kvass: rusks and a water bucket, no fire needed
message.samogon.brewery.no_room: Not enough room: the brewery needs a clear 2×2 area.
message.samogon.brewery.unformed: The brewery is built from four blocks in a 2×2 shape.
message.samogon.rack.no_room: Not enough room: the rack needs a clear 1×2 area two blocks tall.

guide.samogon.brewer.recipes.empty: Beer is brewed in the brewhouse (mash and hop boil); it ferments in the beer barrel.

guide.samogon.brewer.style.origin.schwar: roasted malt and water, bottom fermentation
guide.samogon.brewer.style.origin.bock: malt, water and honey, bottom fermentation
guide.samogon.brewer.recipe.step.mash.ba: Mash: malt and a water bucket, 20 seconds.
guide.samogon.brewer.recipe.step.mash.wh: Mash: wheat and a water bucket, 20 seconds.
guide.samogon.brewer.recipe.step.mash.ro: Mash: roasted malt and a water bucket, 20 seconds.
guide.samogon.brewer.recipe.step.boil: Boil with hops over heat, 30 seconds.
guide.samogon.brewer.recipe.step.ferment: Ferment in the beer barrel with yeast at 8–38 °C, 3 min 20 sec.
Ferment in the beer barrel with yeast and honey at 8–38 °C, 3 min 20 sec.

guide.samogon.brewer.page.overview.title: Full cycle
guide.samogon.brewer.page.overview.lead: Four steps, fire and time. From malt to a glass of beer.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.overview.flow3: hopped wort and yeast → beer in a mug
guide.samogon.brewer.page.overview.tip: Right-click opens the brewery panel. Sparkles mean ready.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.title: Raw materials
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.malt: Malt: grain charge, +4 to mash quality.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.wheat: Wheat: a soft grain for the wheat styles.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.roasted: Roasted malt: the dark grain for the dark style, +4 to mash quality.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.hops: Hops: bitterness and aroma; seeds sometimes hide in ferns — plant them on farmland.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.yeast: Yeast: starts the fermentation of hopped wort in the beer barrel.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.water: Water bucket: returns as an empty bucket after the mash.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.honey: Honey: a fermentation additive for the honey style.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.berries: Berries: a fermentation additive for the berry style.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.apple: Apple: a fermentation additive for the apple style.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.cocoa: Cocoa beans: with roasted malt they give the porter.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.summary: One mash yields 1000 units of wort; one mug holds 500. Warmth gives an ale, cold a lager.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.malt.tip: The brewery works only with its own ingredients: the tun and barrel reject brew batches.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.mash.title: Mash
guide.samogon.brewer.page.mash.step1: Put malt, wheat or roasted malt into the raw slot.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.mash.step2: Pour the water: a water bucket into the additive slot.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.mash.step3: The mash runs 20 seconds; no fire is needed for the mash.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.mash.tip: The finished wort stays in the kettle or is bottled.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.mash.note: An empty bottle in the output slot is filled with the current stage.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.boil.title: Boil
guide.samogon.brewer.page.boil.step1: The kettle must already hold wort from the mash.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.boil.step2: Put hops into the additive slot.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.boil.step3: Light a fire directly below the brewery: the boil runs 30 seconds.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.boil.tip: Without fire below the kettle the boil is paused.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.boil.note: Boiling with hops raises the quality of the wort.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.kvass.title: Kvass
guide.samogon.brewer.page.kvass.step1: Dry the rusks: bake bread in a furnace or over a campfire.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.kvass.step2: Put rusks into the raw slot, a water bucket into the additive slot and pick the Kvass tab.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.kvass.step3: Kvass wort steeps 20 seconds without fire; bottle it into glass bottles.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.kvass.step4: Add yeast in the beer barrel: a warm fermentation gives kvass of about 1 %% ABV; draw it into wooden mugs.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.kvass.tip: Kvass is almost alcohol-free; pour a mug into a shot glass or cup to serve it properly.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.ferment.title: Ferment
8–38 °C; below 14 °C a lager, above an ale
guide.samogon.brewer.page.ferment.step1: Drain the hopped wort from the brewery into the beer fermentation barrel.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.ferment.step2: Put yeast into the additive slot; honey, berries, an apple, hops or cocoa beans in the raw slot set the style.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.ferment.step3: Fermentation runs 3 min 20 sec and gives beer of about 5 %% ABV in a wooden mug.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.ferment.tip: Outside 8–38 °C fermentation stalls; heat and cold hurt quality. Cold below 14 °C gives a lager.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.bottle.title: Bottling
guide.samogon.brewer.page.bottle.step1: Place an empty wooden mug in the output slot for beer, and a glass bottle for wort.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.bottle.step2: The brewery fills a bottle with wort, the beer barrel fills a mug with beer.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.bottle.step3: Take the vessels while the machine still holds a drink.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.bottle.tip: Beer is poured only into wooden mugs; wort goes into glass bottles.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.trouble.title: Troubleshooting
guide.samogon.brewer.page.trouble.heat: The kettle does not boil: fire or a lit campfire must be directly below the brewery.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.trouble.mash: The mash will not start: the raw slot needs malt, wheat or roasted malt, the additive slot a water bucket.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.trouble.boil: The boil is silent: the kettle needs finished wort, plus hops and fire below.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.trouble.fermen: Fermentation stalled: the beer barrel needs hopped wort and yeast, kept at 8–38 °C.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.trouble.bottle: The mug is not filled: beer needs one wooden mug in the output, wort a glass bottle.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.trouble.room: The brewery is not built: clear a 2×2 area.
guide.samogon.brewer.page.trouble.tip: Empty-hand right-click opens the panel. Light and sparkles mean ready.

desc.samogon.grape_must: Fresh grape juice straight from the press. Ferment it in the barrel.
desc.samogon.wine: Wine is older than writing: grapes were fermented in the Neolithic, and ancient Greeks drank it only diluted — neat wine was barbaric. Romans carried the vine across Europe, monks preserved it, and today wine is argued over, tasted and described in words nobody understands.
desc.samogon.sparkling_wine: Sparkling wine was invented by monks who could not stop a second fermentation in the bottle. The mistake was first cursed, then called champagne and sold for more. Today bubbles are the main attraction: the cork pops, the mood rises, and so does the price.
desc.samogon.wine.dry: Dry wine is the oldest format: grapes, yeast and time, with no sugar and no additives. Greeks diluted it with water, Romans carried the vine across Europe, and monks spent centuries perfecting the cellar. Everything else is the winemaker's imagination.
desc.samogon.wine.oaked: Oak barrels became popular for practical reasons: they were easy to store and ship, and the wine emerged darker, softer and touched with vanilla. The Romans noticed this early; modern winemakers still argue over how much oak is wine and how much is furniture.
desc.samogon.wine.off_dry: Off-dry wine appeared where grapes did not fully ripen: acidity remained, sugar remained, and the result was lively and easy to drink. In Germany such wines were called 'halbtrocken', and they became so popular that people started making them on purpose. Do not ask whether it is off-dry or semi-sweet.
desc.samogon.wine.semi_sweet: Semi-sweet wine is a compromise between dryness and dessert: enough sugar to soften the acidity, but not enough to eat with a spoon. In the Soviet Union such wines were mass-market and beloved, while sommeliers pretended not to notice their popularity. They still pair well with almost any dinner.
desc.samogon.wine.sweet: Sweet wines were made in antiquity: the rich had honey, the poor had underripe grapes, and winemakers had a harvest to save. Later people learned to stop fermentation and add sugar, and sweet wine became a dessert. The argument over whether it is wine or jam can go on forever.
desc.samogon.wine.dessert: Dessert wines are wines that survived a great deal of sugar: from Sauternes to Malaga, they were made from overripe or dried grapes. The sweeter they are, the less people drink at once, but the longer they remember. Serve them in small glasses so the dessert lasts.
desc.samogon.wine.vermouth: Vermouth was invented in 18th-century Turin as a wormwood medicine, but it turned into an aperitif. Italians steeped herbs in white wine, the French in red, and bartenders added gin and called it a martini. The lesson: if a drink is bitter enough, sooner or later people will enjoy it.
desc.samogon.wine.mulled: Mulled wine was heated by the Romans with honey and spices to survive winter. In the Middle Ages hot wine counted as medicine; today it is a remedy for bad weather and ice-rink queues. Do not let it boil, or the alcohol will leave before the guests.
desc.samogon.wine.sangria: Sangria was born in Spain as a way to refresh wine in the heat: water, fruit, ice and some sugar. Later brandy and oranges joined in, and the drink became something to enjoy on a terrace while arguing whether it is 'real' sangria. The real one is in your glass.
desc.samogon.wine.honeyed: Honeyed wine was known to ancient Greeks and Slavs: honey was sweeter than sugar, and sugar did not exist yet. It was drunk at feasts, used to treat colds and offered to the gods. Modern winemakers add honey to bring back that warmth — and to justify a second bottle.
desc.samogon.wine.cuvee: Cuvee means a wine blended from several varieties: the winemaker combines them like a perfumer, so one adds body, another acidity, a third aroma. In Bordeaux such blends became the norm, in Champagne the foundation of the style. Do not ask which variety rules: it will take offence.
desc.samogon.wine.port: Port was invented in 17th-century Portugal when the English needed a substitute for French wine: grape spirit was added to the barrel so the wine would survive the sea voyage. The result was strong, sweet and durable, named after the port of Porto. Port has been a culture ever since.
desc.samogon.wine.sherry: Sherry was born in Andalusia, where wine aged under a layer of 'flor' yeast: it protected the wine from air and gave a special taste. The English loved sherry before, during and after dinner, and Shakespeare mentioned it in his plays. Dry sherry is an aperitif, sweet sherry a dessert.
desc.samogon.sparkling.classic: Classic sparkling wine uses the traditional method: the wine ferments twice in the bottle, the bubbles are natural, and the sediment is removed on a riddling rack. Champagne perfected it, but today England and Crimea use it too. Do not call everything champagne: the French will hear.
desc.samogon.sparkling.blanc_de_blancs: Blanc de Blancs means 'white from whites': a sparkling wine made from white grapes, most often Chardonnay. The style is prized for purity, citrus freshness and the ability to age longer than some marriages. The name sounds expensive, and that is no accident: a good Blanc de Blancs costs accordingly.
desc.samogon.sparkling.rose: Rose sparkling wine was made by winemakers who wanted both celebration and lightness: brief contact with red grape skins gives the colour, and the second fermentation gives the bubbles. France long considered it frivolous, until it appeared at every society reception. It is the most photogenic drink in the glass.
desc.samogon.sparkling.red: Sparkling red is a rare beast: made from red grapes, it looks like wine in the glass but behaves like champagne. Australia calls it 'sparkling shiraz', Italy has lambrusco, and Burgundy has its own experiments. Serve it chilled, or the bubbles and tannins will start an argument.
tooltip.samogon.machine.pressing: Wine press: grapes + skins switch  must
tooltip.samogon.machine.sparkling: Riddling rack: still wine + sugar  sparkling wine
gui.samogon.button.skin_contact.tooltip: Red grapes kept on the skins give red wine; pressed straight off they give rose
gui.samogon.button.dosage.tooltip: Sweetness of the finished sparkling wine
wine.samogon.cuvee.name: Cuvee (%1$s / %2$s)
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipes.title: Wine recipes
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.dry.name: Dry varietal wine
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.dry.desc: The base wine of any variety: the must ferments on yeast, the wine is racked off the lees and bottled. The grape and the skins set the colour.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.dry.step1: Press grapes into must: red on the skins gives red, off the skins gives rose, white stays white.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.dry.step2: Charge the must into the fermentation barrel and add yeast.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.dry.step3: Bottle the dry wine after fermentation.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.oaked.des: Aging on oak: the chips give vanilla and tannin, the wine rounds out and loses its edge. Best for reds and full whites.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.oaked.ori: dry wine + oak chips -> aging cask
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.oaked.ste: Make a dry wine and charge it into the aging cask.
Put oak chips into the additive slot.
Wait for the cycle: the wine turns oaked and softer.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.off_dry.d: One sugar per bottle: a light residual sweetness of about 4-12 g/l. Sugar goes in after fermentation, in the aging cask.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.off_dry.s: Make a dry wine and charge it into the aging cask.
Put exactly 1 sugar into the additive slot.
Bottle the off-dry wine after the cycle.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.semi_swee: Two or three sugars per bottle: a soft 12-45 g/l sweetness. Good for reds and aromatic whites.
Make a dry wine and charge it into the aging cask.
Put 2 or 3 sugar into the additive slot.
Bottle the semi-sweet wine after the cycle.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.sweet.des: Four to six sugars per bottle: a pronounced sweetness above 45 g/l. Sugar masks acidity and rough notes.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.sweet.ste: Make a dry wine and charge it into the aging cask.
Put 4-6 sugar into the additive slot.
Bottle the sweet wine after the cycle.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.dessert.d: Seven or more sugars per bottle: a thick, liqueur-like wine. In game it stands in for a late harvest or an ice wine.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.dessert.o: dry wine + 7 or more sugar -> dessert
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.dessert.s: Make a dry wine and charge it into the aging cask.
Put 7 or more sugar into the additive slot.
Bottle the dessert wine after the cycle.
An aromatized wine: the dry wine is blended with a botanical bundle. Real vermouth uses wormwood, roots and herbs.
Make a dry wine and charge it into the blending table.
Put a botanical bundle into one of the five slots.
Start the blend: the wine becomes vermouth.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.mulled.de: Spiced wine. In game the spices are cocoa beans, nether wart or blaze powder; sweeten it separately with sugar.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.mulled.st: Make a dry wine and charge it into the blending table.
Add spices: cocoa beans, nether wart or blaze powder.
Start the blend: you get mulled wine.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.sangria.d: Wine with fruit and berries. Apple, melon, pumpkin or berries go into the blend for a light fruity drink.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.sangria.o: dry wine + fruit or berries -> blending table
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.sangria.s: Make a dry wine and charge it into the blending table.
Put fruit or berries into the additive slots.
Start the blend: you get sangria.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.honeyed.d: Wine sweetened and perfumed with honey. Honey softens the acidity and adds a floral note.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.honeyed.s: Make a dry wine and charge it into the blending table.
Put a honey bottle into the additive slot.
Start the blend: you get honeyed wine.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.cuvee.des: A blend of two still wines: a base and a wine of another variety meet on the blending table. The colours add up: red with white gives rose, rose with red gives red, rose with white gives white. A cuvee can still be oaked, sweetened or fortified afterwards.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.cuvee.ori: still wine + a bottle of another wine -> blending table
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.cuvee.ste: Charge the first wine into the blending table: it becomes the base of the cuvee.
Put a bottle of a second wine into the additive slot: another variety brings another character.
Press Blend: the two wines marry at once, with no separate cycle.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.port.name: Port
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.port.desc: A fortified wine: a strong spirit of 30 % ABV or more is added to the dry wine. The spirit stops fermentation and keeps the sweetness; grape brandy such as chacha, brandy or cognac is traditional, but any strong distillate will do. Port is a final style: a finished port is not aromatized.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.port.orig: dry wine + strong spirit -> blending table
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.port.step: Make a dry wine, preferably red, and charge it into the blending table.
Put a bottle of strong spirit (30 % or more) into the additive slot.
Start the blend: you get a port of up to 22 % ABV.
Bottle the port and let it rest: a fortified wine only gains from time in the bottle.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.sherry.de: A fortified wine that is aged on oak first and fortified afterwards. Oxidative aging gives the nutty notes. Sherry is a final style: it is not blended again.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.sherry.or: oaked wine + strong spirit -> blending table
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.sherry.st: Make a dry wine and age it in the cask with oak chips.
Charge the oaked wine into the blending table and add a strong spirit.
Bottle the sherry: the oxidative aging has already given it the nutty notes.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.classic.d: The traditional method: tirage liqueur, second fermentation in the bottle, lees aging, riddling, disgorging and dosage. Any dry white works.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.classic.o: dry white wine + sugar -> bottle rack
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.classic.s: Make a dry white wine from Riesling or another white grape.
Charge the wine into the rack and pick a dosage.
Add sugar and start the second fermentation.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.blanc_de_: Sparkling wine from white grapes only, in game from Chardonnay: fine, acidic and citrusy.
Press Chardonnay and ferment the must into white wine.
Make a dry white wine and charge it into the rack.
Pick a dosage and start the second fermentation.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.rose.name: Rose sparkling
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.rose.desc: Sparkling wine from a rose base: red grapes pressed off the skins. Berry notes and a short aging.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.rose.step: Press red grapes with skin contact turned off.
Ferment a dry rose and charge it into the rack.
Pick a dosage and start the second fermentation.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.red.name: Sparkling red
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.red.desc: A rare style: sparkling wine from red wine on the skins. Full-bodied, with berry acidity and lively bubbles.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.red.step1: Press red grapes on the skins and ferment a dry red.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.red.step2: Charge the red wine into the rack.
guide.samogon.winemaker.recipe.red.step3: Pick a dosage and start the second fermentation.
message.samogon.sparkling.sugar: Need %1$s sugar for the tirage and the dosage.
message.samogon.blend.fortified: This wine is already fortified: it cannot be aromatized or fortified again.
message.samogon.blend.finished: This wine is already aromatized: only a plain wine can be fortified.
message.samogon.blend.cuvee.base: A cuvee needs a bottle of plain still wine as its base.
gui.samogon.hint.press: Grapes: skins = red, no skins = rose

guide.samogon.winemaker.colours.title: Grape varieties
guide.samogon.winemaker.varieties.title: Grape varieties
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.strength: A dry wine reaches about %s %% ABV.
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.note: Age a still wine in the cask; the rack turns it sparkling.
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.red.descr: The classic red: the skins stay with the must, the wine ferments warm and the cask rounds it out.
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.red.step1: Press red grapes with skin contact on.
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.red.step3: Age in the cask, then bottle or put it through the rack.
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.white.des: White grapes never take colour from the skins: the must is pressed straight off and ferments cool.
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.white.ste: Press white grapes; the skin contact button changes nothing.
Bottle it young or give it a short rest in the cask.
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.rose.orig: red grapes, pressed off the skins
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.rose.desc: Rosé is red grapes pressed straight off the skins: a light blush and a cool fermentation.
guide.samogon.winemaker.colour.rose.step: Turn skin contact off and press red grapes.
Bottle it young: rosé gains little from a long cask.
guide.samogon.winemaker.variety.cabernet: A full-bodied red: the skins stay with the must, the wine ferments warm and loves the cask.
Press Cabernet with skin contact on to get red must.
Ferment at 24 °C and age it in the cask.
Bottle it as a still wine or send it to the rack for sparkling.
guide.samogon.winemaker.variety.merlot.d: A softer red that ferments a little cooler than Cabernet and gives a rounder wine.
guide.samogon.winemaker.variety.merlot.s: Press Merlot on the skins for red, or off the skins for rosé.
Good both as a young rosé and as an aged red.
guide.samogon.winemaker.variety.chardonn: A versatile white: the must is pressed straight off and ferments cool.
Press Chardonnay; the skin contact button changes nothing.
Bottle it young or give it a short rest in the cask.
guide.samogon.winemaker.variety.riesling: The coolest white: light, acidic must and a short aging.
Press Riesling straight into white must.
Ferment at 14 °C — warmth costs it its freshness.
Bottle it young; the cask is only worth a couple of cycles.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.overview.le: Wine needs no still. Four vessels carry the grape from the press to a bottle with bubbles.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.overview.fl: wine and oak chips → softer wine
wine, sugar and dosage → sparkling wine
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.overview.ti: Empty-hand right-click opens a machine panel. Sparkles mean the batch is ready.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.grapes.red: Red grapes (Cabernet, Merlot): the skins give colour; charge them into the press.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.grapes.whit: White grapes (Chardonnay, Riesling): always white must, with skins or without.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.grapes.suga: Sugar: the tirage and dosage charge in the bottle rack.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.grapes.yeas: Yeast: starts the primary fermentation in the barrel.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.grapes.bott: Glass bottle: must, wine and sparkling wine are bottled only into it.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.grapes.oak: Oak chips: one handful starts a cask cycle.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.grapes.summ: One press gives 1000 units of must; one bottle holds 750. Each variety makes its own wine and sparkling.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.grapes.tip: Grape seeds drop from grass. Plant them on farmland — the vine climbs red supports and gives bunches.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.press.title: Pressing
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.press.label: PRESS
GRAPES
MUST
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.press.step1: Right-click the press with grapes: red and white both go in.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.press.step2: The skin contact button decides: on gives red from red grapes, off gives rosé.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.press.step3: Pressing takes 10 seconds; a glass bottle takes 750 units of must.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.press.tip: White grapes give white must either way — the button only matters for red.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.press.note: One press yields 1000 units of must.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.ferment.ste: Drain the must into the fermentation barrel and put yeast into the additive slot.
Fermentation runs 5 minutes; stay near the colour's temperature for quality.
The wine loses 6 %% of its volume and comes out dry at 11.5–12.5 %% ABV.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.ferment.tip: Above 34 °C the yeast spoils the wine; below 8 °C fermentation barely moves.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.age.title: Aging
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.age.step1: Charge a dry wine into the aging cask.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.age.step2: Add oak chips to start a cycle; it runs 5 minutes.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.age.step3: Each cycle adds 5 quality, drops 3 impurities and loses 1 %% of the volume.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.age.tip: An aged base makes better sparkling wine; an unaged one loses 4 points in the rack.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.sparkling.s: Charge the rack with a dry still wine.
Pick the dosage with the button: it sets the tirage charge and the sweetness.
Add sugar to the additive slot; 5 minutes cover tirage, lees ageing, riddling and disgorging.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.sparkling.t: The second fermentation adds 1.1 %% ABV. Only glass bottles leave the rack.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.sparkling.n: The dosage can still be changed while the rack runs.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.dosage.lead: Brut nature is the driest, doux the sweetest. The sugar count pays for the tirage and the dosage together.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.dosage.tip: Drier dosages give a quality bonus; doux costs two points.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.dosage.note: The rack reads the dosage at the end, so you can change your mind while it runs.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.trouble.pre: The press refuses the stack: it takes red or white grapes, not must or wine.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.trouble.fer: The barrel refuses must: only winery must goes in, not brewer's wort or wine.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.trouble.yea: Fermentation does not start: yeast belongs in the additive slot.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.trouble.age: The cask will not start: charge a wine in a bottle, then add oak chips.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.trouble.rac: The rack refuses wine: only dry still wine can be charged, not must or sparkling.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.trouble.sug: The rack is silent: the sugar in the additive slot must cover the chosen dosage.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.trouble.tem: The wine tastes thin: the cellar was far from the colour's temperature.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.trouble.tip: Empty-hand right-click opens the panel; the bar, the particles and the sparkles tell the state.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.memo.title: Cheat sheet
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.memo.tools: Panel — empty hand. Sparkles — ready. Thermometer and hydrometer read the batch.
guide.samogon.winemaker.page.memo.safety: A game, not a winemaking manual.
